title: CCDV-F Mock Exam #9
description: Full-length 53-question simulation for Claude Certified Developer - Foundations (120 minutes).

questions.prompt: An agent needs to look up a customer's order status via an internal API, then use that result to decide whether to also check the shipping API. Which pattern describes how the agent should proceed after receiving the order-status tool result?

options.text: Send the tool result back to the model as part of the conversation history so it can decide whether another tool call is needed, repeating this exchange until it produces a final response.

Discard the tool result once it has been used to formulate a reply, since only the current turn's content should remain visible in context and earlier tool outputs would otherwise crowd out reasoning space unnecessarily.
Always call every available tool once per turn regardless of relevance, including the shipping API, so the conversation history stays uniform and no tool result is ever missing from the context.

Ask the user to manually review the order-status result and decide whether the shipping API should be called next, pausing the agent's tool-use loop until the user responds with an explicit instruction.

questions.explanation: This is the standard tool-use loop: append the tool result to the conversation, let the model reason over it, and continue looping until it stops requesting tools. Discarding the result breaks the loop by removing context the model needs, calling every tool regardless of relevance is wasteful and not how tool selection works, and pushing the decision to a human defeats the purpose of an autonomous agent that can decide this itself.

questions.prompt: An integration intermittently receives a rate limit response under load. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Retry immediately until the call succeeds
Treat the response as a permanent failure and surface an error
Retry with exponential backoff and a bounded number of attempts
Lower the request size so the limit is never reached

questions.explanation: Backoff with a retry ceiling relieves the pressure that caused the limit and still fails predictably. Immediate retries (A) worsen the condition, treating it as terminal (B) discards recoverable work, and shrinking requests (D) does not address a rate that is measured in calls.

questions.prompt: What does a stop reason indicating the maximum token limit tell you?

options.text: The input was too long
The request was malformed
The model refused the request
The output was cut off before the model finished

questions.explanation: That stop reason reports that generation hit the output ceiling. An oversized input (A) fails before generation, and neither a malformed request (B) nor a refusal (C) produces this reason

questions.prompt: An HTTP handler stores one `messages` array on the Flask app object. Every customer appends to it. Customer B receives Customer A's account id. What is the defect?

options.text: Missing prompt cache breakpoint
Session hygiene — conversation state was shared across users
`stop_reason: pause_turn`
Using Haiku instead of Opus

questions.explanation: You reused one transcript. Cache and model tier do not leak another customer's id by themselves.

questions.prompt: The SDK returned HTTP 200. The model text looks like JSON but `json.loads` throws. What is the software-engineering lesson?

options.text: HTTP success means the body is valid JSON
You still defensively parse and validate model-produced JSON
Regex is more reliable than a JSON parser
The SDK already validated business rules

questions.explanation: Treat model JSON as untrusted. Regex is brittle. HTTP 200 is not schema-valid billing data.

questions.prompt: Too many few-shot examples mainly risk:

options.text: Automatic 401
Token cost and overfitting to the example surface
Mandatory Batch API
Loss of vision

questions.explanation: Cost plus surface overfitting. Not an auth error.

questions.prompt: Your app must show partial output to users as it's generated, and some responses may exceed 20K output tokens. What must you do?

options.text: Nothing special
Use streaming, since non-streaming risks HTTP timeouts above ~16K tokens
Lower `max_tokens` to 16K
Switch to Haiku

questions.explanation: Non-streaming HTTP clients time out on very long outputs. Lowering `max_tokens` truncates the answer. Haiku is a model choice, not the timeout fix.

questions.prompt: Behavior changed on Monday. Git shows no application commit. A marketplace plugin was left on "latest." What is the most likely cause?

options.text: SSE event order
An unpinned plugin (or dependency) auto-updated
`strict: true`
Haiku being too cheap

questions.explanation: Pin plugins with the model and the prompt as one release. SSE order and `strict` do not change weekend behavior by themselves.

questions.prompt: A regulated team is mapping engineering activities onto the systems lifecycle for a Claude application. Which TWO activities belong in the **deploy** phase? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Deciding that customer data must be processed in a specific region.
Pinning the full model ID and retaining the prior pinned version as a rollback target.
Choosing Amazon Bedrock because the customer already holds its compliance posture there.
Gating promotion on the eval result against the pinned baseline before a version reaches production.
Instrumenting token cost and latency per call in production.

questions.explanation: Deploy owns pinning (full model ID plus a retained prior version as the rollback target) and the eval gate on promotion. Residency is requirements, platform choice is design, production instrumentation is operate.

questions.prompt: A developer is choosing between calling Claude's REST endpoint directly with an HTTP client and using an official SDK. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The SDK reaches a more capable version of the model than raw REST.
The SDK is a thin convenience layer that handles authentication, request construction, retries, and response parsing.
Streaming requires raw REST; SDKs support only synchronous calls.
Using the SDK removes token-based billing.
The SDK and raw REST reach the same API and the same model.

questions.explanation: The SDK is a thin convenience layer over the same REST API handling auth, request construction, retries, and parsing; both paths reach the same API and the same model, and SDKs fully support streaming.

questions.prompt: During an agent's tool-use loop, a tool raises an exception. The developer's code catches it and returns an empty result block to Claude. What is the consequence, and what is the correct handling?

options.text: The empty result safely stops the loop; correct handling is to also log the exception server-side

The model treats the empty result as valid data and continues reasoning on a false premise, producing a confident but wrong answer; correct handling is to return a tool_result with is_error set to true and the error message so the model can react
The API rejects the empty block with a 400 error; correct handling is to retry the tool call with backoff
The model automatically re-invokes the failed tool; correct handling is to strip the failed call from history first

questions.explanation: A tool that drops its error and returns nothing makes the model treat the empty result as valid data and reason on a false premise. Returning the tool_result with is_error: true and the message lets Claude react — try another approach, ask for clarification, or stop — and a visible failure is far easier to catch than a confident wrong answer.

questions.prompt: A regulated EU bank wants an agent that summarizes customer call transcripts for its support team. Which of the following is a valid functional requirement?

options.text: The agent should be fast and accurate.
The agent produces a summary that a human approves before it is stored.
The system must be built using an approved cloud provider.
Transcript data must not leave the EU.

questions.explanation: B is checkable and tied to a specific business-process constraint (human-in-the-loop review). A is not checkable, and C and D are infrastructure requirements, not functional ones.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team is building a loan-underwriting assistant using the Messages API. Each new user turn is sent as a separate request. What must the application do to maintain a coherent multi-turn conversation?

options.text: Nothing — the API automatically remembers prior turns for the same user.
Resend the full prior message history with every request, since the Messages API is stateless.
Open a persistent socket connection that keeps the conversation state alive.
Only send the single most recent user message, since Claude retains context server-side by default.

questions.explanation: The Messages API is stateless: the application is responsible for resending the full conversation history (or the relevant portion of it) on every call.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team notices a response for a returns-processing assistant was cut off mid-sentence, and the API response reports stop_reason: max_tokens. What does this indicate, and what's the right fix?

options.text: The model refused the request; the fix is to change the prompt's wording.
A rate limit was hit; the fix is to back off and retry.
The output hit the configured max_tokens limit before finishing; the fix is to raise max_tokens (or shorten the expected output) appropriately.
The request was malformed; the fix is to resend it unchanged.

questions.explanation: stop_reason: max_tokens means generation was cut off purely because the token limit was reached, not a refusal or an error — raise the limit or reduce the expected output length.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team needs a loan-underwriting assistant to analyze a 90-page loan agreement directly, including its layout and any embedded tables, rather than manually extracting the text first. What is the best-fit integration approach?

options.text: Manually OCR the PDF into plain text and discard the original layout before calling Claude.
Refuse the request, since Claude cannot process document files.
Pass the PDF directly to Claude as a document content block so it can reason over the full document.
Split the PDF into individual words and send them as a list.

questions.explanation: Claude supports document/file input directly, so PDFs can be passed as a content block and analyzed natively — including layout and tables — without a separate manual extraction step.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team needs a returns-processing assistant to compare two images (e.g., before-and-after screenshots) in a single evaluation. What is the correct way to structure the request?

options.text: Include both images as separate content blocks within the same message so Claude can reason over both together.
Convert both images to base64 and concatenate the strings before sending as one image block.
Stitch the two images into a single file outside the API and hope Claude infers there were originally two.
Claude can only accept one image per request, so the two must be evaluated in separate calls with no shared context.

questions.explanation: Multiple images can be included as separate content blocks in one message, letting Claude directly compare or reason across them in a single call.

questions.prompt: While integrating a loan-underwriting assistant, a fintech startup's platform engineering team sees a request fail with HTTP 429 and a rate-limit error. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Treat it as a permanent failure and stop calling the API for this feature entirely.
Silently swallow the error and return an empty response to the user.
Immediately retry the exact same request in a tight loop as fast as possible.
Back off and retry after a delay (ideally with exponential backoff and jitter), respecting any provided retry guidance.

questions.explanation: A 429 indicates a rate limit was hit — the correct response is backing off (typically exponential backoff with jitter) and retrying, not hammering the API or giving up permanently.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team wants application logic in a returns-processing assistant to branch correctly depending on why generation ended — for example, executing a tool when Claude requests one versus simply displaying the final answer. Which field should the application inspect?

options.text: The current system time, to guess whether a tool call is likely.
The length of the response text, inferring intent from character count.
The response's stop_reason field, which distinguishes cases like end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens, and stop_sequence.
The HTTP status code alone, which is always 200 regardless of how generation ended.

questions.explanation: stop_reason tells the application why generation stopped (e.g., tool_use vs end_turn vs max_tokens), and is the correct signal for branching application logic — not status code, text length, or guesswork.

questions.prompt: A research team needs to classify sentiment for 2 million historical customer reviews as part of a one-time data-cleaning project. The results are needed within the next two days, no individual result needs to return quickly, and the team wants to minimize API spend. Which approach is best?

options.text: Submit all 2 million requests synchronously in parallel by opening as many concurrent connections as the client allows, prioritizing the fastest possible wall-clock completion time over cost or rate-limit considerations.
Submit the requests through the Message Batches API, which processes large asynchronous workloads within a completion window at a lower price than synchronous calls.

Use the streaming API for every request so that partial sentiment results can be saved incrementally as tokens arrive, which reduces the effective per-request cost compared to a full synchronous response.

Keep using the synchronous Messages API for all 2 million calls, but reduce max_tokens to 1 on every request so that output token billing is minimized regardless of whether a usable sentiment label is returned.

questions.explanation: This is a latency-tolerant, high-volume, cost-sensitive workload, exactly what the Batches API is built for, and it offers a cost discount. Option A maximizes cost and risks hitting rate limits for no benefit given the relaxed timeline. Option C's streaming doesn't reduce cost. Option D destroys the usefulness of the output and still ignores the batch discount.

questions.prompt: A developer is confused why a coding instruction placed in a project's CLAUDE.md file changes Claude Code's behavior, but placing that same text in a one-off chat message on claude.ai does not have the same persistent effect across future, unrelated conversations. What best explains this?

options.text: claude.ai and Claude Code are built on different, incompatible underlying model weights and tokenization schemes, so an instruction phrased in one interface has no conceptual equivalent in the other and cannot be expected to influence behavior in a different product, regardless of how or where it is stored.

CLAUDE.md is a project-level context file that Claude Code loads automatically into context for every session in that project, giving it persistent, session-spanning authority; a claude.ai chat message is scoped to that single conversation and has no mechanism to persist across separate, unrelated sessions.

claude.ai is designed to ignore substantive user instructions within a session and instead defers entirely to Anthropic's own hidden system prompt for behavioral decisions, which is why a one-off instruction typed into a chat message has no lasting or even immediate effect on its responses.

Claude Code cannot read arbitrary files from the local filesystem during a session, so the presence or absence of a CLAUDE.md file is actually irrelevant to its behavior, and the behavior change the developer observed was most likely just a coincidental variation in the model's sampling rather than any file being loaded into context.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is automatically loaded as persistent project context in every Claude Code session in that project, while a message in a claude.ai chat is scoped to that single conversation with no cross-session persistence mechanism. Option A is false; interfaces differ, but this is not about incompatible model weights. Option C is false; claude.ai does follow user instructions. Option D directly contradicts the documented purpose and function of CLAUDE.md.

questions.prompt: Which task most clearly justifies the most capable model available?

options.text: Deciding a multi-step migration plan across several interacting systems
Extracting a date from a short, well-formed string
Converting a list into title case
Detecting whether a message is in English

questions.explanation: Deep, multi-step reasoning over interacting constraints is where capability differences show. The other three are mechanical or single-signal tasks that a small model handles at a fraction of the cost.

questions.prompt: You need a token count for `claude-sonnet-5` before you pay for the real call. What do you use?

options.text: `tiktoken`
`client.messages.count_tokens(model="claude-sonnet-5", ...)`
`len(text.split())`
Character count divided by 4 from a blog post

questions.explanation: Always Claude's counter for that model. Third-party tokenizers miscount.

questions.prompt: A product serves mixed traffic: ~90% of requests are short factual lookups and label extractions, ~10% are long multi-document synthesis with high cost-of-error. Evals show Haiku holding the bar on the simple traffic and only Opus holding it on the synthesis traffic. Which serving strategy does the course support?

options.text: Sonnet for all traffic — one balanced model avoids routing complexity and covers both ends adequately.
Opus for all traffic — the deciding constraint is never failing the synthesis requests.
Route by a cheap task signal: Haiku default on the simple traffic, with an Opus override on the synthesis requests — pay for capability only where the eval shows it is needed.
Haiku for all traffic, with extended thinking enabled at high effort to close the gap on synthesis.

questions.explanation: Mixed traffic with eval evidence on both ends calls for routing: the cheap tier where the eval holds, an Opus override where only it passes. A single model either overpays 90% of traffic or fails the hard 10%.

questions.prompt: A long multi-turn agent session keeps accumulating history and tool results. What symptoms should the team expect, and which budget is at fault?

options.text: The model silently drops the oldest turns to make room, so the session continues but quietly loses early context.

The context window is a fixed token budget: an already-oversized input is rejected with an error before generation, while a request that reaches the ceiling mid-generation returns truncated output with a model_context_window_exceeded stop reason — so a session that ran fine in testing can fail once inputs grow, and the application must trim or summarize history.
The symptom is slower sampling, and the budget at fault is the temperature setting, which must be lowered as the session grows.
There is no fixed budget; the window expands automatically to hold whatever history accumulates.

questions.explanation: The context window is a fixed budget: oversized input errors before generation, and hitting the ceiling mid-generation returns truncated output with a model_context_window_exceeded stop reason. History is never silently dropped, so trimming or summarizing is the application's job.

questions.prompt: A multi-step agent plans a dependent refactor where a wrong early step is expensive, and an eval shows Sonnet missing the bar on the hardest cases. Which model choice is best, and what is the deciding constraint?

options.text: Sonnet — the deciding constraint is cost efficiency on a long agent run
Opus — the deciding constraint is quality on hard reasoning where the cost of a wrong answer is high
Haiku — the deciding constraint is speed across many sequential steps
Sonnet — the deciding constraint is latency on dependent steps

questions.explanation: The deciding constraint is quality on hard reasoning where the cost of a wrong answer is high, and the eval shows the step up from Sonnet is needed. Model changes are promoted on a measured eval score, not on assumption.

questions.prompt: A conversation in a returns-processing assistant has grown very long and is approaching the model's context window limit, and an e-commerce platform's backend team notices Claude starting to lose track of details from early in the thread. What is the most appropriate fix?

options.text: Summarize or trim older turns to keep the most relevant context within the window, rather than sending the entire unbounded history forever.
Ignore the issue, since context windows are unlimited in practice.
Increase temperature to help the model remember more.
Switch to a smaller, cheaper model, which will not experience this issue any differently.

questions.explanation: Context window management — summarizing or trimming older turns to preserve the most relevant information — is the correct fix when a long conversation risks exceeding (or crowding) the context window.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team must choose a model tier for a loan-underwriting assistant where both cost and latency matter a great deal, and the budget is fixed, but the task still requires solid quality. What best describes the correct approach?

options.text: Always pick the cheapest tier regardless of whether it meets the quality bar.
Pick a tier at random since all tiers perform identically in practice.
Weigh cost, latency, and quality together, and validate that the chosen tier actually meets the required bar for this specific task before committing.
Always pick the most capable tier regardless of cost or latency constraints.

questions.explanation: Model selection is a genuine tradeoff between cost, latency, and quality for the specific task — the right approach validates the chosen tier against the actual quality bar rather than defaulting to an extreme.

questions.prompt: A subagent is introduced to a working pipeline and quality drops. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The subagent needs a larger model
The subagent lacks context the main agent held, and the handoff did not carry it
Subagents are unsuitable for pipelines
The pipeline needs more subagents

questions.explanation: Delegation trades context for isolation, and quality falls when the handoff omits what the subtask needed. A larger model (A) cannot supply missing context, subagents are widely used in pipelines (C), and adding more (D) multiplies the same fault.

questions.prompt: Orchestrator-workers: the high-level plan → dispatch → synthesize is fixed in your code. The orchestrator call picks the subtasks. This is:

options.text: A fully autonomous agent with no workflow
Still a workflow
Invalid; only humans may split tasks
CMA-only

questions.explanation: Code still owns the pattern. That is a workflow, not a free agent loop.

questions.prompt: A healthcare startup wants to run a PHI-processing agent on Claude Managed Agents because the managed sandbox removes operational burden. The workload requires a HIPAA BAA. What should the team do?

options.text: Use Managed Agents — Anthropic's managed environment satisfies HIPAA obligations by default.
Use Managed Agents with session storage disabled in the agent definition.

Rule out Managed Agents — its sessions are stateful and stored server-side, so it is not currently eligible for ZDR or a HIPAA BAA — and build on the Agent SDK or a raw loop on a covered configuration.
Prototype on Managed Agents and migrate only if the compliance audit objects.

questions.explanation: Managed Agent sessions are stateful and stored server-side, so the offering is not currently eligible for ZDR or a HIPAA BAA. The compliance constraint picks the wiring path: Agent SDK or a raw loop on a covered configuration.

questions.prompt: A team has a specialized review checklist that applies only to a subset of tasks. They currently keep it in CLAUDE.md, which loads into every Claude Code session and inflates context even when irrelevant. What pattern should they move it to?

options.text: A Skill: a SKILL.md file whose name and description load at startup, with the full instructions loaded only when a request matches the description
In-context instructions pasted at the start of every conversation, since these persist across sessions
A subagent, since subagents automatically inherit all Skills and instructions from the parent session
A larger CLAUDE.md with headers, since Claude only reads the sections relevant to the task

questions.explanation: A Skill loads its full instructions only when a request matches its description; only the name and description load at startup, unlike CLAUDE.md which loads every session unconditionally. Note that subagents do not automatically inherit Skills — they must be listed explicitly.

questions.prompt: A B2B analytics SaaS platform team is automating account audit logs processing for a report-generation assistant: every case follows the same fixed sequence (extract fields, check policy rules, route exceptions to a human queue, generate a summary), and success is easy to verify. Which architecture is the best fit?

options.text: A deterministic workflow that calls Claude only at defined steps in a known sequence.
A fully autonomous agent that decides each next action for every case.
A long-running agent that must retain memory of every case indefinitely.
A manager agent that delegates every single case to specialized subagents.

questions.explanation: When the sequence and branching are known and fixed and success is easy to verify, a deterministic workflow is the better fit — an open-ended agent would add unnecessary variability the task doesn't need.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team needs to process a large set of independent return requests where each case can be handled without any dependency on the others. Which orchestration pattern is most efficient?

options.text: Route every case through a single subagent one at a time regardless of independence.
Force every case through a single shared conversation thread to preserve order.
Fan the independent cases out to run in parallel, since there is no dependency between them.
Process every case strictly one at a time in a single sequential chain.

questions.explanation: When subtasks are genuinely independent, parallelization (fanning them out concurrently) is the efficient orchestration pattern rather than an unnecessary sequential chain.

questions.prompt: A hospital system's patient-portal engineering team is running a long-lived agent for a clinical intake assistant that needs to recall decisions and progress from earlier sessions, not just the current conversation. What capability addresses this?

options.text: Agent memory, which persists relevant state or context across sessions rather than starting from a blank slate each time.
Ignoring the need, since agents cannot retain any information across sessions.
Increasing temperature so the agent 'remembers' more creatively.
A larger max_tokens setting for the current request only.

questions.explanation: Agent memory is the mechanism for persisting relevant state or prior context across sessions, distinct from the current conversation's context window.

questions.prompt: With compaction enabled, a long-running agent gradually loses track of decisions taken early in the session. The loop appends the assistant's extracted text string to history on each turn. What is the defect?

options.text: Compaction keeps only the most recent turns by design, so early decisions are expected to be dropped entirely.
The compaction blocks in each response are discarded, so the API has nothing to substitute for compacted history.
Compaction summaries are delivered out of band and must be fetched separately once a session crosses a threshold.
Compaction is disabled automatically once tool results dominate a transcript, and the loop never re-enables it.

questions.explanation: This is the append-the-full-content-list rule again, and it bites hardest here. The response carries compaction blocks that the API uses to stand in for compacted history on the next request. Extracting only the text string throws them away, so the conversation silently loses its compaction state and the early context it was meant to preserve.

questions.prompt: A long-running assistant begins contradicting itself and forgetting recent constraints. Inspection shows the context is nearly full of verbose tool outputs. What is the correct remedy?

options.text: Increase temperature to encourage variety
Prune and summarize tool outputs, compact history, and isolate subtasks so the working context stays lean
Repeat the system prompt after every turn
Reduce max_tokens on each response

questions.explanation: Context drift and bloat are managed by pruning, compaction, and isolation

questions.prompt: What is the critical implementation detail when using beta compaction?

options.text: You must lower `max_tokens`
You must append the full `response.content` (including the compaction block) back into `messages`, not just extracted text
Compaction only works with vision
You must disable caching

questions.explanation: The compaction block is part of the mechanism. Text-only echo breaks it. Vision and cache are unrelated requirements.

questions.prompt: A short, well-specified classification task already returns the right answer zero-shot. What does adding three worked examples to the prompt most likely do?

options.text: Improves accuracy substantially.
Adds token cost on every call for little or no gain.
Changes the model being used.
Disables sampling.

questions.explanation: Add examples when the output shape is wrong, not when zero-shot already works; each example costs tokens on every call for little or no gain here.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team wants a returns-processing assistant to consistently adopt a specific persona and follow standing behavioral rules on every call, separate from whatever the user happens to type. Where does this belong?

options.text: Repeated inside every user message in slightly different wording.
Nowhere in particular — persona and standing rules cannot be set via prompting.
In a separate, disconnected request sent before the real one.
In the system prompt, since it's the dedicated place for persistent, call-spanning instructions.

questions.explanation: The system prompt is the right home for persistent role and behavioral rules that should apply on every call, distinct from the specific per-turn user request.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team wants a loan-underwriting assistant to consistently adopt a specific persona and follow standing behavioral rules on every call, separate from whatever the user happens to type. Where does this belong?

options.text: Repeated inside every user message in slightly different wording.
In the system prompt, since it's the dedicated place for persistent, call-spanning instructions.
Nowhere in particular — persona and standing rules cannot be set via prompting.
In a separate, disconnected request sent before the real one.

questions.explanation: The system prompt is the right home for persistent role and behavioral rules that should apply on every call, distinct from the specific per-turn user request.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team is prompting a returns-processing assistant with a 45-page vendor contract plus a short final question about it. Per Claude's documented long-context guidance, where should the long reference document be placed relative to the instructions/question?

options.text: Near the top of the prompt, with the specific instructions or question placed at the end.
It doesn't matter at all where long reference material is placed.
Interleaved randomly with the instructions throughout the prompt.
Always after the question, never before it.

questions.explanation: Documented long-context guidance recommends placing long reference material near the top of the prompt, with instructions or the specific question at the end, for the most reliable results.

questions.prompt: A company needs to classify millions of short customer feedback snippets per day as positive, negative, or neutral. The task itself is straightforward, and the team's top priorities are low latency and low cost at very high volume. Which model tier is the best fit?

options.text: The largest, most capable model tier available, because classification accuracy must always be maximized regardless of cost or latency.
The fastest, most cost-effective, lightweight model tier, since the task is simple and high-volume, where latency and cost matter more than deep reasoning capability.

A custom-trained model from outside the Claude family entirely, since the Claude model family was designed primarily for open-ended generation and lacks the architecture needed to perform reliable text classification tasks.

The mid-tier balanced model, and only that tier, because the lightweight fast model is architecturally incapable of performing any text classification task and would simply fail or refuse to return a label.

questions.explanation: For simple, extremely high-volume classification where speed and cost dominate the decision, the lightweight/fast model tier is the right choice since the task doesn't require the deeper reasoning the larger tiers offer at higher cost and latency. Option A ignores the stated cost/latency priorities, option C is factually wrong since Claude models handle classification well, and option D incorrectly claims the lightweight tier can't classify text at all.

questions.prompt: Which describes the correct relationship between an MCP server and the applications that use it?

options.text: The server exposes tools and resources that multiple clients connect to, maintained independently of any one application
Each application embeds its own copy of the server code
The server replaces the Messages API
The server must run in the same process as the model

questions.explanation: An MCP server is a reusable, independently maintained capability that multiple clients share

questions.prompt: Eighty tools. Accuracy is dropping. Tool search: which is correct?

options.text: Defer the search tool
Keep search loaded, set `defer_loading` on cold tools, still send all schemas
Remove deferred schemas from `tools`
Disable descriptions so prompts stay small

questions.explanation: Search tool stays loaded. Deferred tools still listed. Descriptions are how search works.

questions.prompt: A code-search service runs on company infrastructure, and every engineer who clones the repository should get access automatically. Which transport-and-scope combination is correct?

options.text: stdio transport committed to `.mcp.json` at project scope, so the launch command travels with the repo.
HTTP transport at project scope — commit the server URL to `.mcp.json` at the repo root; a stdio entry would look shareable but runs as a subprocess on one machine.
HTTP transport at user scope, configured once in each engineer's personal settings.
stdio transport at user scope, since personal configuration is the most reliable.

questions.explanation: A remotely hosted, team-shared service is HTTP transport at project scope: the URL committed in `.mcp.json` travels with the clone. A stdio entry in `.mcp.json` looks shareable but launches a subprocess that exists on one machine.

questions.prompt: A developer discovers that a service-account API key was committed inline in the `Authorization` header of `.mcp.json` and pushed to the shared repository two days ago. Which TWO actions are required? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Rotate the key immediately, treating the committed credential as compromised
Overwrite the file in a later commit with the key removed, which clears it from the repository
Update `.mcp.json` to reference the credential as an environment variable (e.g., `Bearer ${WAREHOUSE_MCP_TOKEN}`) so the value never travels with the file
Switch the server from HTTP to stdio transport so headers are no longer needed
Move the server entry to `.claude/settings.local.json` and leave the existing key in place

questions.explanation: A credential committed to a repository enters history, where overwriting the file in a later commit does not remove it, so the key must be treated as compromised and rotated; the configuration must then reference the value through an environment variable so the file no longer carries the secret. Overwriting alone, changing transport, or relocating the config leaves the exposure in place.

questions.prompt: A hospital system's patient-portal engineering team is building an agent for a clinical intake assistant that needs to pull capabilities from several different external MCP servers (e.g., one for internal data, one for a third-party API) at once. What role does the agent play in this setup?

options.text: The agent must reimplement each external system's API from scratch instead of using MCP at all.
The agent acts as an MCP client, connecting to multiple MCP servers to access their exposed tools/resources through a standardized protocol.
The agent becomes an MCP server itself and has no client role.
MCP only supports connecting to exactly one server per agent, so this setup isn't possible.

questions.explanation: An agent that connects to multiple MCP servers to use their exposed tools/resources is acting as an MCP client — the standardized protocol is what avoids bespoke per-server integration code.

questions.prompt: A research assistant built on Claude produces a well-written literature summary that cites five academic papers with specific titles, authors, and years. The citations read as fluent and authoritative. Before publishing the summary, what should the team do?

options.text: Publish the summary as-is without further checking, since citations that include specific titles, named authors, and precise years are detailed enough to be treated as verified and trustworthy.
Independently verify each citation against a real bibliographic source (e.g., a database or search) before relying on or publishing it, since fluent, specific-sounding output can still be fabricated.
Ask Claude to restate the same five citations in a more confident, assertive tone as a self-check, treating an increase in confident phrasing as evidence the citation details are accurate.
Remove all five citations from the summary entirely, on the position that any citation generated by an AI model is inherently unusable regardless of whether it could be independently verified.

questions.explanation: Fluency and specificity are not evidence of accuracy -- models can generate plausible-sounding but fabricated citations, so independent verification against a real source is the necessary safeguard before publication. Trusting detail or specificity as a proxy for truth is exactly the failure mode being tested. Asking the model to restate the claim more confidently does nothing to verify factual accuracy. Blanket removal is an overreaction; verified citations can still be valid and useful.

questions.prompt: What is the correct way to enforce a rule that must hold 100% of the time (e.g., "never run `rm -rf`")?

options.text: A strongly worded system prompt instruction
A deterministic hook/code-level check, since prompting is probabilistic
Ask the model to double-check itself
Increase `effort`

questions.explanation: Prompts are probabilistic. Injection can override them. Hooks are code. Self-check and `effort` are still the model.

questions.prompt: A developer must assemble the minimal secure configuration for an agent that fetches untrusted web content and writes to a single protected path under a scoped identity. Which TWO pieces belong in that configuration? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A PreToolUse hook that runs before write_file executes, denies any write outside /workspace/output, and logs the attempt
An API key pulled from an environment variable or secret manager rather than committed configuration
A system-prompt line instructing the model to ignore any instructions found in fetched pages, relied on as the enforcement layer
A retry wrapper with exponential backoff around the write call
Broad write access for the agent, with a weekly review of the audit log to catch misuse

questions.explanation: The PreToolUse hook is enforcement, not convention: it blocks the write before execution and logs it, and the environment-variable secret keeps the credential out of repository history where it could never be cleanly rotated. A prompt instruction is not a security control, a retry wrapper is error handling rather than a boundary, and broad access with after-the-fact log review violates least privilege.  ---

questions.prompt: A user of a clinical intake assistant tries to get Claude to ignore its safety guidelines by framing the request as a fictional roleplay scenario. What is the correct posture for the application to take?

options.text: Disable logging so the attempted jailbreak isn't recorded.
Maintain the same safety guardrails regardless of framing, and add application-level checks rather than relying on the model's judgment alone.
Assume jailbreak attempts are not a real concern once a system prompt exists.
Treat the fictional framing as a legitimate exception and relax safety guardrails for the roleplay.

questions.explanation: Jailbreak attempts often use reframing (roleplay, hypotheticals) to bypass guidelines — the correct posture keeps guardrails consistent regardless of framing, backed by application-level checks rather than the model alone.

questions.prompt: Your CI pipeline runs Claude Code non-interactively and must parse its output. Which invocation fits?

options.text: Interactive mode with output piped to a file
The print flag with a JSON output format and a schema, so results are machine-readable and validated
Plan mode with a human approver
A wrapper that screen-scrapes the terminal

questions.explanation: Headless CI use means non-interactive invocation with structured, schema-validated output

questions.prompt: A developer is building a data-analysis assistant that must run Python calculations, such as computing summary statistics, on CSV files that users upload during a conversation. The Claude API already offers a hosted, sandboxed code execution capability for exactly this purpose. Which approach best fits the requirement?

options.text: Build a custom tool that shells out to a Python interpreter running on infrastructure the developer stands up, hardens, and secures themselves, giving full control over the execution environment.
Build and maintain an MCP server that exposes a run_python tool backed by a sandbox the developer hosts, so the execution environment can be tailored exactly to the analysis assistant's needs.
Create a Skill containing example Python snippets and statistical formulas so Claude can reason through the summary statistics step by step in its response without ever executing code.
Declare the built-in code execution tool in the request so Claude can run Python in Anthropic's managed, sandboxed environment

questions.explanation: The built-in code execution tool is a server-side tool that already runs in an Anthropic-managed, sandboxed container, so declaring it is the correct, lowest-effort, and most secure choice for exactly this need. Building a custom tool around a self-hosted Python sandbox reinvents a capability Anthropic already provides and adds real security and operational burden. An MCP server wrapping a self-hosted sandbox has the same drawback. A Skill only supplies instructions or snippets; it does not execute code, so it can't reliably perform actual computation on uploaded data.
